owner.name: QQ Chen
owner.headline: I start from a pain point and use AI to ship the thing that fixes it.
owner.blurb: Eight products in a year, built on evenings and weekends. Every one started as a problem I or someone near me actually had — then AI-assisted development took it from idea to something people use. I own the vision, the roadmap and the release, not every line of code.

products.name: Dutch Exam Ace
products.subtitle: Dutch integration-exam platform
products.tagline: I built it to pass the Dutch integration exam myself. I passed. It has drawn 9,858 visitors since January.
products.role: Solo — product, backend, AI grading, monetisation
products.problem: The Dutch integration exam (Inburgeringsexamen) is compulsory for residency, and almost no preparation material exists in Chinese. Candidates study from Dutch-language material for an exam they are taking precisely because they do not yet speak Dutch.
products.what: A full preparation platform covering all four exam skills plus KNM: 50+ past-paper questions, 14 writing templates, 1,000+ high-frequency words, mock speaking exams, and AI grading for both writing and speaking against the CEFR A2 / DUO criteria. Core content is permanently free.
products.hard: Grading speech and writing in a language the learner is failing at, and having the score be trustworthy. Early versions were too generous, which is worse than useless — a candidate who thinks they are ready walks into the real exam and fails. Rebuilding the speaking scorer to report real fluency signals honestly took several rounds.
highlights: 9,858 visitors and 26,667 page views since January, for an audience as narrow as it gets: Chinese speakers sitting the Dutch integration exam. Visitors rather than registered users — that is what the analytics measure.
2.7 pages per visit across the whole period — people arrive and work through material rather than bouncing. Traffic took off around 11 April and has held since, entirely through organic search.
AI grading for writing and speaking built against the published DUO A2 criteria — my approximation of them, and the UI says so rather than implying an official rubric.
Made the speaking scorer honest after finding it inflated results — a generous score is worse than no score when someone is deciding whether to book the real exam.
Core content is free and stays free — the pieces that cost money to run are funded separately so the free path never degrades.
Rate limiting on the speech-grading endpoints fails closed, so a limiter outage degrades access rather than the bill. The other AI endpoints have not had the same pass.
products.business: Core content is permanently free and always will be; an optional resource pack covers running costs. Reaches its audience entirely through organic search — no paid acquisition, no ads.
products.card: I built it to pass the Dutch integration exam myself. I passed. It has drawn 9,858 visitors since January.
products.journey: I could not find Dutch exam material in my own language → built the platform → passed the exam → 9,858 visitors since January.
products.impact: 9,858 visitors this year · I passed the exam using it · organic search only
products.roleShort: Product · backend · AI grading pipeline · access model

products.name: TingZhai
products.subtitle: AI notes for podcast listeners
products.tagline: Hands busy? Say "note" out loud and the last 60 seconds is captured, transcribed and filed.
products.role: Solo — product, backend, iOS, App Store submission
products.problem: People listen to podcasts while cooking, driving or running — exactly when reaching for the phone is impossible. So the one good idea per episode is lost. Existing apps require a tap, which means they only work when you weren't really busy.
products.what: An iOS app and web app that plays podcasts and lets you capture a moment by speaking a single word. It rewinds 60 seconds, transcribes that span, has an LLM title and summarise it, then schedules it for spaced review at 1, 3, 7 and 14 days.
products.hard: Two things. First, wake-word detection that runs on-device, works while audio is playing through the same speaker, and does not fire during normal conversation. Second, keeping AI cost viable when every listener processes the same episodes.
highlights: Custom on-device wake word instead of Siri, so playback is never interrupted. Validated against 127,000 characters of real Chinese podcast transcripts: false triggers went from 38 to 0 after switching from single-character matching to a debounced multi-word matcher.

Cross-tenant transcript cache keyed on feed URL plus episode ID: one episode costs AI money once, no matter how many users process it. 86% cache hit rate, 7.07× reuse, US$0.82 per episode all-in, measured over production traffic.
Spaced repetition (SM-2) on captured highlights — I have not found another podcast app that schedules review of what you saved.

Ran an adversarial pre-submission review with a second AI agent. It caught two real App Store rejection risks I had written myself: a described feature the iOS build did not have, and a privacy label that under-declared audio collection.
products.business: Free tier gives every registered user a monthly AI processing allowance. The limit is set from measured cost per episode, not guessed — which is why the free tier can be generous without becoming unbounded.
products.card: Hands busy? Say "note" out loud and the last 60 seconds is captured, transcribed and filed.
products.journey: I kept losing the one good idea per episode because my hands were busy → built voice capture that never interrupts playback → three App Store releases.
products.impact: On the App Store, v1.7 · US$0.82 per episode at 86% cache hit
products.roleShort: Product · backend · iOS · App Store submission

products.name: Woordjes & Tango
products.subtitle: One vocabulary engine, two languages, both on the App Store
products.status: App Store · Dutch v1.12 · Japanese v1.3
products.tagline: I built the Dutch one for my own exam. Shipping the Japanese one was content work, not a rewrite — 95% of the code is shared.
products.role: Solo — product, backend, iOS, App Store submission
products.problem: Vocabulary apps teach words you will never be tested on. Exam candidates and language learners need the intersection of what is frequent and what is examinable — and for Dutch aimed at Chinese speakers, that barely existed.
products.what: Two iOS and web apps on one engine. Dutch: 2,000 high-frequency words levelled A1/A2/B1 against the official exam syllabus. Japanese: 10,000 words across JLPT N5–N1 plus grammar cards, on the same spaced-repetition scheduler.
products.hard: Deciding what to teach, and proving the engine generalised. Frequency lists alone give function words; syllabus lists give words nobody says. And the only honest way to prove a system is reusable is to ship the second one.
highlights: Japanese levelling rebuilt against a 44,000-word frequency corpus after finding advanced kanji compounds filed as intermediate. Re-scored against that corpus, no N1-frequency word remained in a lower band and the N3 bucket shrank from 39% to 21% of the deck.
Concrete nouns auto-illustrated with generated images: roughly 300 images for about US$2, applied only where illustration actually helps.
Second language shipped with 95% of the code shared — the reuse claim was tested by shipping, not argued.
products.business: Both free, no ads, no tracking. Built for my own exam first.
products.journey: I was failing my own Dutch vocabulary → built the deck I needed → then proved the engine generalised by shipping it again in Japanese.
products.impact: Two languages on the App Store off one engine · 95% shared code
products.roleShort: Product · content strategy · iOS · App Store submission

approach.title: I let the test overrule me
approach.body: The readable transcript view drifted out of sync with the audio. I diagnosed it, wrote the fix, and wrote a test to prove the fix worked. The test said my fix was worse than the bug — 40 seconds off where the old code was 22.
approach.evidence: I had been mapping paragraphs by character count. A forty-second pause contains almost no characters, so the character axis could not see it at all. The second attempt anchored on the words themselves and the same test passed nine cases. Measurement is only worth the cost if you let it change what you ship.

approach.title: I make two AI agents review each other, and I check the reviewer before I trust it
approach.body: Claude and Codex work the same repository under one written rule: the reviewer is never the author, and only the reviewer closes a ticket. Before relying on that I tested the second agent with a deliberate trap — asking it to close its own ticket, with a plausible excuse about being short of time.
approach.evidence: It refused and cited the rule by line number. That told me the written constraint was enough and saved me building the enforcement layer I had already designed. The same pairing later caught two App Store rejection risks in copy I had written myself.

approach.title: The feature I was proudest of was the one real use proved wrong
approach.body: The hands-free wake word was the product's own name — obvious choice, and it demoed perfectly. In real kitchens it kept failing: the name is an invented word, so the speech model had never learned it and kept hearing a common word that sounds similar.
approach.evidence: I replaced it with ordinary words people already say — note, record, highlight — which felt like giving up the brand and was the right call. Same pattern with Bluetooth: it only surfaced when someone cooked with a speaker instead of the phone. Neither problem was findable at a desk.

approach.title: Deciding not to build is part of the job
approach.body: Keeping the voice mode alive on a locked screen was possible and I had the design ready. I worked through who would actually be in that situation and what it cost in battery.
approach.evidence: Two paths already covered both real cases, so I did not build it and wrote down why. The same call killed a planned enforcement layer once testing showed it was unnecessary. Scope you do not build is scope you never have to maintain.

casestudy.title: Grading speech the model could not hear
casestudy.blurb: An AI scoring feature was confidently reporting pronunciation errors it had no structural way to detect. Finding that changed the product copy, the prompt, the audio pipeline, the free tier and the error messages — in that order.
